notesDetails.title: Busy-Polling Background Tasks Burnt ~31% of Total Cost ($1.68)
bullets: Whenever a run_command call exceeded the 10-second synchronous wait cap (WaitMsBeforeAsync: 10000), the harness backgrounded it (24 times total) and automatically emitted a system_message wakeup when the command finished.

Instead of ending its turn and waiting for that system_message, the agent polled manage_task(Action: "status") 99 times (plus 6 kill calls = 105 manage_task calls, or 27.1% of all 388 LLM turns) every ~3.5 seconds.

During the final mix test runs in S7 and Post-S7 (which took 102.1s and 101.9s at steps 671 and 738), the agent polled manage_task 24 times and 22 times in a row while context was at its peak (~250k–268k tokens).

Impact: Those 105 manage_task turns alone consumed 19.44M cached tokens and 253k uncached input tokens, costing $1.68 (30.9% of the entire $5.43 run). Stopping and waiting for the reactive system_message would have cut LLM calls from 388 to ~283 and saved ~$1.68.

notesDetails.title: Erlang/Elixir SIGINT (Ctrl-C) Handling Dominated Complexity (47% of Calls)
bullets: S1 + S7 accounted for 183 of 388 LLM calls (47.2%) and 52.5% of all thinking tokens (36,341 / 69,199).

Why: In S1 (steps 28–123), the agent tried calling :os.set_signal(:sigint, :handle) and System.trap_signal(:sigint, ...) and hit BEAM's built-in restriction: Erlang's signal server intercepts SIGINT for the interactive BREAK menu and Elixir's System.trap_signal/3 explicitly disallows :sigint via guard clauses.

Four of the agent's 5 search_web calls were spent researching BEAM/escript SIGINT handling before it arrived at the working architecture in cb: a POSIX shell wrapper that traps INT, runs escript with +Bi (disabling the BEAM break handler), and forwards SIGTERM to the BEAM process so System.trap_signal(:sigterm, ...) can cleanly stop the benchmark loop.
While prototyping this with erl -help and Python pty.openpty() scripts (steps 38, 65, 73, 111, 596, 605), 6 commands hung waiting on terminal I/O and had to be killed after 10–23s.

notesDetails.title: Context Caching Saved 87% on Input Cost ($36.72 Saved)
bullets: 98.11% cache hit ratio: Out of 55,453,077 total prompt tokens sent across the 388 turns, 54,406,484 were served from cache (cache_read_tokens).

Zero mid-run cache invalidations: Only 7 steps had cache_read_tokens: 0—all within the first 15 steps (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 13, 15) while the initial prompt was warming up. All 381 subsequent LLM calls achieved a cache hit.

Dollar impact: Without implicit caching, 55.45M input tokens at $0.75/1M would have cost $41.59 (total run $42.16). Caching reduced input cost to $4.87 ($0.78 uncached + $4.08 cached), saving $36.72 (82% of total cost).

notesDetails.title: Compounding Effect: Sequential 5s Integration Tests × 268k Context Window
bullets: Context grew steadily from 10,704 tokens (step 1) to 268,770 tokens (step 796), spending the last 112 LLM calls above 200k tokens.

At the same time, because each slice added real-time CLI integration tests (5-second benchmark loops and 2-second timeouts), mix test wall-clock time grew from 0.75s (S1) → 12.7s (S3) → 27.5s (S4) → 51.4s (S5) → 102.1s (S7).

Running full mix test suites late in the conversation when context was ~250k+ tokens—combined with the 10s backgrounding threshold—caused the final verification (Post-S7, just 2 test runs) to cost $0.74, more than S2 ($0.20), S4 ($0.52), S5 ($0.59), or S6 ($0.38).

Takeaway for test design: Running targeted unit/simulated-clock tests during iteration and reserving full 5-second real-clock CLI suite runs (mix test --only integration) for final checks keeps mix test under the 10s threshold and avoids background-polling spirals.

notesDetails.title: High Edit Precision (99.2% Tool Success Rate)
